card4r

card4r gives R access to the card collection of hydroclimatic variables: low flows, floods, seasonality, climate change, computed on your own data.

The collection and the engine are not rewritten in R, they are called. A data frame goes in, data frames and their metadata come out. Which means the numbers are the same, whichever language you call them from.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("lou-heraut/card4r")

There is nothing else to install. On the first call, card4r provisions the Python environment it needs on its own (interpreter, numpy, pandas, scipy, then card and stase), through reticulate. Expect a few hundred megabytes and a network connection, once. Nothing is installed system-wide: it lives in reticulate’s cache and can be deleted at any time, it will be rebuilt on the next call.

Each release of card4r pins the exact versions of card and stase it calls, by tag rather than by branch. Two people running the same version of card4r therefore run the same code, and card_config() says which:

card_config()
# python       : ~/.cache/R/reticulate/uv/cache/.../bin/python
# card         : 0.7.0
# card commit  : …
# stase        : 0.6.3
# stase commit : …

If you would rather supply your own Python, point at it before loading the package and card4r will provision nothing:

Sys.setenv(RETICULATE_PYTHON = "/path/to/python")

That is also the way to go behind a proxy that blocks the download, or on a machine without network access.

Using card4r

A first extraction

The example below runs on a real record: the Yzeron at Craponne, a periurban catchment west of Lyon, gauged since 1970. The data comes from Hub’Eau, the French open hydrological API, which needs no key.

library(card4r)
# install.packages("jsonlite")

url <- paste0("https://hubeau.eaufrance.fr/api/v2/hydrometrie/obs_elab",
              "?code_entite=V301501001&grandeur_hydro_elab=QmnJ",
              "&date_debut_obs_elab=1970-01-01&size=20000")
obs <- jsonlite::fromJSON(url)$data

data <- data.frame(date = as.Date(obs$date_obs_elab),
                   Q    = obs$resultat_obs_elab / 1000,   # Hub'Eau serves L/s
                   id   = obs$code_station)
# 19273 daily values, 1970-01-01 to 2022-10-26

Three columns are all card needs: a date, a series identifier, and the numeric columns the cards ask for (Q for discharge, T for temperature, R for precipitation). Then:

res <- card_extract(data, cards = c("QA", "VCN10"))

head(res$data$QA, 3)
#           id       date        QA
# 1 V301501001 1969-09-01       NaN
# 2 V301501001 1970-09-01 0.2967836
# 3 V301501001 1971-09-01 0.2786175

head(res$data$VCN10, 3)
#           id       date  VCN10
# 1 V301501001 1969-02-01    NaN
# 2 V301501001 1970-02-01 0.0155
# 3 V301501001 1971-02-01 0.0213

One data.frame per card. The first row is empty because the record starts mid-year, and the two cards do not use the same window: QA runs over the hydrological year starting in September, VCN10 starts its year at the month of highest flows, February here.

These are the same values, digit for digit, as the Python example in card’s README. That is the whole point of the package: one definition, one engine, two languages.

Alongside the values, res$meta holds one row per variable produced:

res$meta[, c("variable_en", "unit_en", "name_en", "version")]
#   variable_en      unit_en                                      name_en version
# 1          QA m^{3}.s^{-1}                  Annual mean daily discharge     1.0
# 2       VCN10 m^{3}.s^{-1} Annual minimum of 10-day mean daily discharge     1.1

It also carries the description, the classification, the method step by step and both languages, plus what it takes to trace the computation, which the last section of this part covers.

Finding your variable

The whole collection is browsable online: the catalogue, and in French. From R:

card_list()                          # every variable, one per row
card_list(phenomenon = "low flows")  # by hydrological phenomenon
card_list(output = "series")         # a series, versus a scalar or a curve
card_list(statistic = "minimum")     # by the operation that produced it
card_list(statistic = "change")      # the change between two periods
card_info("VCN10", lang = "en")      # one card, drawn

Facets accept English as well as French (output = "series" or output = "série"). statistic and aspect are orthogonal: VCN10 and tVCN10 are both a minimum, one being its value and the other its date.

Card names are systematic and can be read rather than looked up: QJXA is discharge, daily, maximum, annual. The grammar is summarised at the top of the catalogue and given in full in NOMENCLATURE.md.

Trend 

tr <- card_trend(res)

tr$data$VCN10[, c("id", "h", "p", "a", "a_relative")]
#           id    h          p             a a_relative
# 1 V301501001 TRUE 0.05671581 -0.0001151515  -1.069519

The low flows of this catchment decline by about 1.1 % per year over the record. h says whether the trend is significant at the requested level, 0.1 by default, a is the Sen slope in the unit of the variable per year, and a_relative the same as a percentage of the mean.

card_trend() takes the object card_extract() returned, and not a table you rebuilt yourself: it needs the time column as card handed it over, before card4r turned it into Date for you.

What a result says about itself 

res$meta[1, c("version", "swhid", "card_commit", "stase_commit")]
#   version                swhid card_commit stase_commit
# 1     1.0 swh:1:cnt:e1197d4d…           …            …

version is that of the card, which changes as soon as its outputs change, and swhid identifies the card file itself in Software Heritage. The two commits identify the software that ran: a version number designates a unique state only on the day it is published, a commit always does.

An exported result therefore says what produced it, which is what it takes to cite it or to replay it years later. card_config() prints the same without running a computation.

What card4r does not do, and will not do

  • Write a card in R. A card is a YAML file of the collection, and that is what keeps a single definition for both languages. Writing or contributing one happens in card, and the card you write there is immediately usable from here.
  • Re-export the hydrological functions (compute_FDC, get_BFI…). They remain the internal machinery of the cards.

These two limits are not gaps: they are what keeps the package a bridge instead of a second engine to maintain. The day a function had to cross the bridge, the cost would go from a weekend to a year.

Coming from the CARD package

CARD is the original R package, where card comes from. It still installs and is not going away, but it is no longer developed: the living version is on the card side.

Switching does not change your results: the two packages are run on the same series in this package’s test suite, so the agreement is measured at every release rather than claimed here.

CARD (R) card4r
CARD_extraction(data, CARD_name = ...) card_extract(data, cards = ...)
CARD_list_all() card_list()
CARD_management(...) card_info(...)

The expand_overwrite, rmNApct, rm_duplicates and dev arguments of CARD_extraction have no counterpart: they went away with the port. card4r does not accept them, rather than ignore them silently.

The ecosystem

card the card collection, in Python
stase the aggregation and trend engine
card4r the same collection, called from R (you are here)
card-api the web service, on Hub’Eau discharge data
CARD-R · EXstat the historical R packages, superseded

Licence and citation

GPL-3. The collection, the engine and this package each have their own CITATION.cff. Cite the cards you used, with their version, which res$meta gives you.
